body:
Are wereally reducing the attack surface?
Because `innerHTML = '<svg onload=alert(1)>'` still works (and any other event attribute)

(wrong @freddyb, btw)

Hrm. I feel like I tested that, but I must be holding it wrong.

FWIW, I'd be fine with breaking event handlers as well. :)

It seems very unlikely to me that it would be web compatible to break event handlers.

As for `srcdoc` -- what about `<iframe src="data:text/html,<script>...">`?

> It seems very unlikely to me that it would be web compatible to break event handlers.

Yeah. My enthusiasm is waning a bit after that realization. I suspect that whatever numbers I can gather will probably show that usage is high enough to make changing the default behavior untenable. :(

That said, I'd still like to add the flag during parsing, as this still seems valuable as an opt-in hardening mechanism.

> As for srcdoc -- what about `<iframe src="data:text/html,<script>...">`?

I'm less concerned about that as it runs in a unique origin, but I agree that it's a vector to consider.

For that matter, <iframe src="javascript:alert(1)"> will get the job done. 

But if sites could opt in to this behavior, it would be like a finer grained version of CSP w/out unsafe-line. In which case, maybe think about whether this is the best set of behaviors to block.

@rsussland: Indeed. This isn't the extent of what I'd suggest as an opt-in hardening mechanism, but I do think that adding a flag during parsing that captures the parser's scripting flag will be a component of a wider restriction. I'm still hammering things out with @arturjanc and others, but I think I'd like to introduce some sort of "parser-inserted, but by a script" flag that could allow developers to limit `document.write*` as well as the various fragment-processing setters (`innerHTML`, `outerHTML`, `createContextualFragment`, and so on).

When we have a more concrete proposal, I expect we'll put it up on the WebAppSec list.
(Thoughts on scope and etc, welcome, of course, but it's a bit of a side-topic to this issue in particular.)

Also, a motivation for the narrow case that I neglected to note above: `<iframe srcdoc>` is one of the few ways in which CSP nonces can be reused via fragment injection. That is, in the presence of `script-src 'nonce-abc'`, an attacker who can figure out how to exfiltrate the secret token can still cause script execution if they can find an `innerHTML`-style sink that accepts`<iframe srcdoc='<script nonce=abc>yay();</script>'></iframe>` (`document.write` is, of course, another, but it's far too widely used to consider changing the default behavior).

I don't think this is fundamentally different from `<iframe src="blob://stuff">` being inserted via innerHTML.  Or heck, `<iframe src="some-relative-url">`.

Is the intent to turn off scripting entirely for all loads in an `<iframe>` inserted via innerHTML?  Or to only turn it off for srcdoc loaded in such an iframe?  What happens if an `<iframe>` is inserted via innerHTML with no attributes and then much later the srcdoc attribute is set?  Or the iframe is navigated to some other URL?

In general, the "do not run script" behavior of innerHTML is not a security feature.  It's a compat feature, and it was introduced solely because people had a tendency to append things by doing `body.innerHTML += stuff` (which is a bad pattern for all sorts of reasons, of course).  I don't think we should be trying to shoehorn security properties in here, because as pointed out above that ends up in a whack-a-mole of stupendous proportions....

> but it's far too widely used to consider changing the default behavior

And you don't think innerHTML is?
Ah, I guess with opt-in we could consider something, but it's still not clear to me what the "something" should be.

In general I agree with Boris that the current `innerHTML` behavior isn't a security feature (because of event handlers, javascript URIs, etc, all of which will execute script as a result of the assignment). But there are two aspects of the change Mike is proposing that lead to useful security benefits:

1. We already have a mechanism that prevents the execution of event handlers, javascript: URIs, and most other inline scripts: CSP without 'unsafe-inline'. This means that sites with CSP are already free of such markup so they will not need to change if they want to opt into this "do not run script" mode.
2. There are only a few remaining patterns which allow the execution of scripts via parser-based DOM APIs; iframe#srcdoc is the main one which allows an attacker to do so in the context of the current origin via an innerHTML injection. Such patterns are very rare in real applications (because it's a hacky way to add a new script and much better APIs exist to do so, e.g. `createElement('script')`) so this will not require significant refactoring of existing code.

The big picture is that we could provide developers a mode that guarantees that no new scripts will be added via parser-based JS DOM APIs like innerHTML (which are the cause of the vast majority of DOM XSS), and most applications with CSP will be able to adopt this with little effort.

> CSP without 'unsafe-inline'

That would block the "script inside srcdoc" thing as well, modulo whatever the story is with nonces, right?

I'm open to the idea of preventing script injection here, but scoping it down to just that will end up with a pretty hacky and fragile setup, I expect.  I'd be happy to be proved wrong, of course.

> That would block the "script inside srcdoc" thing as well, modulo whatever the story is with nonces, right?

In theory yes, but in practice no ;-) A large majority of CSP policies have insecure script-src whitelists because of JSONP, Angular on CDNs, [etc](https://research.google.com/pubs/pub45542.html). An attacker with an innerHTML injection in apps with such policies can currently use iframe#srcdoc to load external scripts from whitelisted domains and bypass the policy. A "do not run script via parser-based DOM APIs" mode would prevent the exploitation of innerHTML-based XSS also in apps with whitelist-based policies.

Having defense-in-depth against nonce reuse is the direct reason to think about this, but I don't think it's the only one.

I introduced this poorly, and then was a bit overly enthusiastic about breaking things in my response to @mozfreddyb, and further conflated multiple problems in my response to @rsussland. Sorry for dragging the conversation off the rails.

_This_ bug is fairly narrowly scoped. My claim is that `el.innerHTML = "<script>yay();</script>";` is the same as `el.innerHTML = "<iframe srcdoc='<script>yay();</script>'></iframe>";`, and that `el.innerHTML = "<script src='yay.js'></script>";` is the same as `el.innerHTML = "<iframe srcdoc='<script src="yay.js"></script>'></iframe>";`. Because they have the same practical implications for code execution, I'd suggest that they should be treated the same when injected into the page. If script doesn't execute in one, it shouldn't execute in the other, and vice-versa. If y'all agree with that claim, wonderful! If not, we should talk about it a little bit more.

If we can agree on the assertions above, then the concrete change I'd suggest would be something along the lines of the following:

1.  Add a flag to `HTMLIFrameElement` denoting whether it was constructed by the [HTML fragment parsing algorithm](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#html-fragment-parsing-algorithm).
2.  When instantiating [an IFrame srcdoc document](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#an-iframe-srcdoc-document), set a similar flag based on its [browsing context container](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#browsing-context-container)'s flag (we'd probably need to cascade this as well, so maybe putting it on the browsing context or something would be more reasonable).
3.  When [preparing script](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#prepare-a-script), check the document's flag. If it shows that the document was indirectly constructed from a fragment, treat the script as [already started](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#already-started).

I suspect that `<iframe srcdoc>` has low-enough usage in conjunction with `innerHTML` that this kind of change could be made without disruption.

To @arturjanc's points: I agree that we'd almost certainly want an opt-in for some broader changes that I think would be reasonable to make, and I'll do my best to explain those in a future bug once we've sketched out in a bit more detail what we'd actually like to do.

> If y'all agree with that claim, wonderful

I don't agree at all, for two reasons.

First,  one of these patterns executes the script sync (for the inline script case), and one does not.  So if you do 15 appends to innerHTML without returning to the event loop, one will run the script 15 times and the other will run it only once.

Second, and more importantly, the scripts are run in different globals.  And whereas (re)running the script in the main global is likely to break (exceptions thrown, etc), running the script in the subframe is more likely to actually be _needed_ for things to continue to work as expected.

That is, in the `innerHTML += foo` case, these two situations have totally different behavior and semantics in terms of outcome.  Yes, they both "execute script", but with totally different effects!

> Because they have the same practical implications for code execution

Again, you're focusing on the "does script run at all?" end of things.  I agree that the two situations are fairly equivalent for that purpose.  But, and I can't stress this enough, the reason the innerHTML setter doesn't run scripts isn't because we want to prevent script injection.  It's for compat with pages that do `innerHTML += foo`.  

And in terms of the actual _behavior_ once the script runs, the practical implications of the two cases are totally different.

As noted in the thread, there's several ways how scripting can be introduced via iframes:

```
<iframe srcdoc="<script>">
<iframe src="data:text/html,<script>">
<iframe src="javascript:">
```

And one can trigger that through `innerHTML` and `document.write`. This issue proposes to disable only one of them, and only via `innerHTML`. That might be surprising to the authors , and so far I only see benefits for CSP'ed websites (and only the ones that have a DOM XSS sink in `innerHTML`). 

What speaks for it, is that perhaps the actual usage of that pattern is small; I don't know though if it's worth complicating the web platform for the authors. What might be better, is the more complete opt-in (e.g. via CSP) solution in which all parser-inserted vectors have scripting disabled.

I think there are two things here:

1. innerHTML not running script elements is purely for backcompat. It doesn't get security without considerable more hardening. I wish we didn't have it, but there's nothing we can do about it now.
2. There is a potential security feature here, but it would need to disable considerably more than script elements (e.g. event handlers). Relatedly, WebKit and Chromium based browsers do some sanitization of content on copy-paste to avoid copy-paste social engineering based XSS. I don't know about other browsers. I could imagine adding a mode on pages that just disables all the features instead of forcing stripping them from the markup.

Basically, what isn't already covered by CSP here? Is it just that you want the behavior to be there by default?

https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-csp/issues/191 has some background explaining the benefit of having this in CSP. Essentially, injections into a DOM API can still allow script execution if the CSP has a bypassable whitelist (most policies do: https://research.google.com/pubs/pub45542.html) or if the attacker has a way to exfiltrate the nonce in a nonce-based policy.

Adding a keyword like in https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-csp/issues/191 can prevent such attacks because all script elements added via parser-based DOM APIs would be inert. The change suggested by Mike here would make adopting this keyword easier because it would remove the main pattern via which `<script>` elements can be added by a parser-based API and still execute (since `innerHTML` does not execute them and `document.write` is ugly and is less common in modern apps that can benefit from CSP).

Note that the main benefit here is for sites which adopt (or want to adopt) CSP so we can assume they don't have inline event handlers or `javascript:` URIs.
Isn't the point that the attacker can inject inline event handlers or `javascript:` URLs (etc) equally well as they can inject a script tag in a srcdoc iframe?

As @bzbarsky and others have noted, I don't think disabling script execution just inside a `srcdoc` document would buy us much.

WebKit, for example, has a special API to strip out event handlers in order to disable script execution even when the user interacts with the content. Something like that is needed for the parsed content to be "truly" safe.

@zcorpan, @rniwa -- the utility of this comes in when the page uses CSP, in which case both inline event handlers and `javascript:` URIs are disabled, so inserting `<script>` elements is pretty much the only way to  add scripts via a parser-inserted API.

@arturjanc: That wasn't in the original proposal nor was it clear that everyone advocating for the feature wanted to have it only in the context of a new CSP header.

Having said that, I can see it may work as a new CSP policy. Nevertheless, as others pointed out, `about:` and `data:` can also run scripts so those things need to be prohibited as well, not just `srcdoc` so I withstand with my original statement that "disabling script execution just inside a srcdoc document would buy us much".

@rniwa You're right that it wasn't clearly explained; I think it's mostly because @mikewest wanted to "normalize" the HTML behavior first so that the CSP feature would be less likely to introduce a change in behavior. If people write code such as `document.body.innerHTML = '<iframe srcdoc="<script>..."</iframe>'` then they will have to refactor it when they adopt CSP or it will break; it's just one more thing to worry about, and there seemed to be little reason to allow it in the first place (except for what @bzbarsky said above).

Re: `data:`  and `about:` URIs, CSP (without `'unsafe-inline'`) disables _all_ inline scripts, so the only way to execute a script via e.g. an innerHTML assignment is to add a new `script` element or `link#rel=import`. Note that scripts inside data: URIs execute in a null origin so they are not subject to the page's CSP, and you similarly shouldn't be able to inject a same-origin script via markup with an `about:` URI -- if that were possible it would be a bypass of existing CSP protections against inline script execution.

If I understand properly, the proposal is then to amend a web platform in order to minimize the possibility that introducing CSP will cause breakage? That change, however, brings breakage possibility, with no real security benefits for all non-CSP websites.

To me, this change should be governed by CSP itself, as it only is security-relevant in that context. For example `iframe.srcdoc=<script>`vector could only be enabled when `unsafe-inline` keyword is used. Or another keyword could manage this. It really feels like a corner case that is only CSP-relevant.

That's a fair point; I believe the assumption was that if creating a script in the same document via an assignment to `innerHTML` doesn't execute it, it would be consistent to also not execute it if the script is added inside an `iframe#srcdoc`. But it seems there are legitimate concerns about this line of thinking.

A slight drawback of preventing execution only when CSP is enabled is that a fairly obscure feature of the platform will behave differently with CSP, which will likely be surprising to developers, and we could avoid this altogether (because `innerHTML = "<iframe srcdoc='<script>...'>"` is a fairly uncommon, awkward pattern). But maybe that's indeed the easiest solution.

@arturjanc, this is actually an argument for it (to be part of CSP). CSP by its nature introduces additional restrictions, and changes how script execution, resource loading and other features work (by prohibiting what is usually allowed). Inline handlers do not work, for example, unless the CSP includes a given keyword. 

It feels more natural to introduce this breaking behavior into sites that opted-in to adhere to the policy. In CSP spec itself, it can be made backwards-compatible (by e.g. adding `stop-scripts-in-iframe-srcdoc` keyword) or safe-by-default (by e.g. merging it with `unsafe-inline`) - likely a decision that can be made based on actual usage of this vector.
Just for reference, I believe CSP without unsafe-inline already prevents `<script>` with no src in iframe@srcdoc running, because the srcdoc document uses the same CSP as its parent.

This makes sense to me overall -- CSP adopters are used to making changes to their applications so we can introduce one more pattern which will require refactoring. I see that the "it's uncommon so let's change the default" argument cuts both ways and perhaps "it's uncommon so it won't cause CSP adopters a lot of refactoring pain" is a more reasonable stance. Based on the discussion here my tacit assumption is that no-one is particularly upset at the prospect of having a CSP opt-in which will enable blocking such parser-inserted scripts.

@mikewest It seems like the best way to go is to specify the behavior in https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-csp/issues/191 and control this at the CSP level?

Re-reading this issue, it seems there was opposition to changing `innerHTML` as proposed here. Since https://github.com/w3c/webappsec-csp/issues/191 exists to explore a fix on the CSP side, I think this issue can be closed.
